<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="11" type="chapter">
               <ns0:head>CHAP. XI.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p>NOw a certain man was sick, <ns0:hi>named</ns0:hi> Lazarus of Bethany <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Bethany,</ns0:hi> (as appeareth by <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 18.) <ns0:hi>was nigh unto Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> not wholly at two miles distance from it: but our Saviour was at this time in <ns0:hi>Iudea,</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 7. he saith to his Disciples, <ns0:hi>Let us go into Iudea.</ns0:hi> Again, he was at this time in <ns0:hi>Galilee,</ns0:hi> or in <ns0:hi>Peraea</ns0:hi>: and we shall find <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 17. That <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> had been in his grave four days, before our Savi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />our got thither: So as we must allow at least six or seven days betwixt the time when Christ heard of <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> his Sickness, and the time when our Saviour came to <ns0:hi>Bethany.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, the town of Mary and her sister Martha <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">This <ns0:hi>B<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>thany</ns0:hi> is here onely described to us, as the place where <ns0:hi>Martha</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mary</ns0:hi> lived, or at least where they were born: Some think that <ns0:hi>Bethany</ns0:hi> was onely a part of the Mount <ns0:hi>Olivet</ns0:hi>; but others more probably, think that it was some little Town or City, standing within that part of the Mount <ns0:hi>Olivet</ns0:hi>; for it is here called a Town, and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 10.38, 39. the place where these two Sisters lived, is called a <ns0:hi>Village.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 (It was <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> Mary which anointed the Lord with ointment, and wiped his feet with her hair <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">We read of a Woman, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 7.38. that came behind our Saviour while he was at dinner, in the House of <ns0:hi>Simon</ns0:hi> the Pharisee; brought an Alabaster box of Ointment, stood at his feet behind him weeping, washing his feet with her tears, and wiping them with her hair; but it appears by the story, she had been before a notorious Sinner. We read of another Woman, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 26.6, 7. <ns0:hi>Mar.</ns0:hi> 14.3. that poured a box of Ointment on our Saviours head, as he was at din<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ner in the House of <ns0:hi>Simon</ns0:hi> the Leper: but we in those two Evangelists, read nothing of her washing his feet with her tears, or wiping them with her hair; but in the next <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> of this Gospel, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 3. we have a story, which (whether it be the same with the other or no, I cannot tell) is that doubtless to which this verse referreth: The Names and circumstances much agree. There were other <ns0:hi>Maries,</ns0:hi> (for <ns0:hi>Mary</ns0:hi> was a very ordinary name among them) but this was that <ns0:hi>Mary</ns0:hi> which is mentioned <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 12.3. that anointed the Lord with Ointment, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> It was her brother was Sick.</ns0:note>, whose brother Lazarus was sick.)</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 Therefore his sisters sent unto him, saying, Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest, is sick <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">Christ (as was said before) seemeth to have been very familiar at the House of these two Sisters, and often to have made them his Hostesses; and if it should appear by this verse, that in those visits he had shewed particular kindnesses to this their brother <ns0:hi>Lazarus,</ns0:hi> who was now Sick, this makes them stile their Brother, <ns0:hi>him whom thou lovest.</ns0:hi> They plead no merits either of their own or his; but onely plead with him for his own goodness and love. Nor do they ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />press in particular, what they desired for their Brother, though it is easily understood by their representation of his state and condition.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 When Jesus heard <ns0:hi>that,</ns0:hi> he said, This sick<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness is not unto death <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">God hath not sent this Sickness upon <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> to de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />termine his being upon the Earth; or such a separation of the Soul of <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> from his Body, as there shall be no re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />union of it before the general Resurrection, (which is our or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dinary Notion of Death) God hath not sent this Sickness for that purpose</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 9.3. ver. 40.</ns0:note> but for the glory of God; that the Son of God might be glorified thereby <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">but that he might be glorified by his Son, rai<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sing him from the dead: God is glorified, when his Son is glorified; and Christ is glorified, when his Divine Power is manifested, so as men acknowledge him to be what indeed he is.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">He doubtless loved them with a special distinguishing love; as persons chose in him to Eternal Life before the foun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dation of the World, given unto him by an Eternal Dona<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, called by him with an effectual calling, to own and receive him as their Saviour; but this text seemeth to speak of him as loving this family, with an human love, which in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clineth man to a complacency in an object beloved; he had a kindness for the whole family: They had shewed him kind<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness in his state of humiliation; and he loved those that so loved him, <ns0:hi>Pro.</ns0:hi> 8.17.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 When he had heard therefore that he was sick, he abode two days still in the same place where he was <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Though he loved him and his Sisters, with a tender love, yet he did not presently go to them, to comfort <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> and <ns0:hi>Martha</ns0:hi> in their sorrow; nor yet to cure <ns0:hi>Lazarus,</ns0:hi> and prevent his Death; but staid still two days in the place where he was. He loved <ns0:hi>Mary,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Martha,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Lazarus,</ns0:hi> but he more loved the Honour and Glory of his Father, which was to be manifested in his raising of <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> from the dead; we must not judge of Christs love to us, by his more external dispensations of Providence; nor judge that he doth not love us, because he doth not presently come in to our help, at our times, and in such ways and methods as we would think reasonable.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 Then after that saith he to <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> disciples, Let us go into Judea again <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">This lets us know, that Christ was not in <ns0:hi>Iudea,</ns0:hi> when he received the tidings of <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> his Sickness, but in <ns0:hi>Peraea</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Galilee</ns0:hi>; but he presently upon it, takes up thoughts of returning again into that Province, and indeed he was now preparing for his last journey thither; however the Sickness of <ns0:hi>Lazarus,</ns0:hi> and his raising from the dead; was one occasion of his so soon going up; from which his Disciples would have discouraged him, as followeth.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 <ns0:hi>His</ns0:hi> disciples say unto him, Master, the Jews of late sought to stone thee; and goest thou thi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther again <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">See <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 10.31. There were not three months elap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed, since the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> had so sought to have stoned him; and there was no reason for him to think, that their fury was in any whit abated. We read in the other Evangelists, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 16.22. of other words they used (<ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> especially) to disswade our Saviour from this journy to <ns0:hi>Ierusalem.</ns0:hi> They were afraid for their <ns0:hi>Master,</ns0:hi> and they were afraid also for themselves.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 Jesus answered, Are there not twelve hours in the day? If any man walk in the day, he stumbleth not, because he seeth the light of this world <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Look as in the day there are twelve hours, in which the Sun shineth, and by giving its light, directs men in their courses, so as they know how to guide their feet; and do not stumble, because they have the light of the Sun, which God hath ordained, to direct men that walk up and down in the world.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 But <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 12.3<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> if a man walk in the night, he stumbleth, because there is no light in him <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">And there is a night also, wherein if men walk, they will be very prone to stumble, because they are in darkness, and have no light to guide their feet. So there is a set-time, for all the issues of men; a time for their peace and liberty, and a time for their troubles and sufferings. God Rules and Governs the World, whiles men are in their callings and places faithfully discharging their trust, and finishing the work which God hath given them to do; and their time is not come, for their glorifying of God by suffering: they shall not stumble, nor be given up to the rage of their eagerest Enemies; they are in their callings and places, and God will be light unto them: But when their working-time is over, and the time of their night is come, then they will stumble; because then God withdraweth his light from them, they are not then under such a special Protection of God, who hath done his work by, and with them. This is as much as he had said before, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 8.20. <ns0:hi>No man laid hands on him, for his hour was not yet come:</ns0:hi> The twelve hours of his day were not all spent. This duty digested, is of infinite use to quiet the Spirits of Gods People in the worst of times; every man hath his <ns0:hi>twelve hours,</ns0:hi> his day and set time, to honour God upon the stage of the World; he shall not stumble, he shall not miscarry while those hours are spent<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> he shall not die, he shall not be disabled for duty, so long as God hath ought for him to do<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> but every man hath his night too, when he must not expect to con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />verse in the World, without stumbling.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 These things said he: and after that, he saith unto them, Our friend Lazarus <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 9.24<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> sleepeth <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">There is such an Analogy betwixt <ns0:hi>Death</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Sleep,</ns0:hi> that there is nothing more ordinary than to express <ns0:hi>Death</ns0:hi> by <ns0:hi>Sleep</ns0:hi> in Scriptures<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>Deut</ns0:hi> 31.16. 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 7.12. 1 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 1.21. 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 20.21 <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 7.21. and 14.12. <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 12.2. and in a multitude of other Texts, both in the Old Testament, and in the New; so as it was evident our Saviour meant he was dead, which he knew as he was God, though as yet he had received no relation of it from the friends of the deceas<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed.</ns0:note>, but I go; that I may awake him out of sleep <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">But I go (saith our Saviour) to raise him up again from the dead, which he calls awaking him; pursuing the former <ns0:hi>Metaphor,</ns0:hi> where he had compared Death to a Sleep.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:353" />12 Then said his disciples, Lord, if he sleep, he shall do well <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Sleeping moderately is a good sign, we know, in most diseases; this makes the Disciples say, that if <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> slept, he should do well.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 Howbeit Jesus spake of his death: but they th<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>ught that he had spoken of taking of rest in sleep <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">But that the Disciples should not understand our Savi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />our, not speaking of ordinary sleep, but of Death, is won<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derful, considering that there is nothing more ordinary in Holy Writ, than to read of Death expressed under this No<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion; but possibly by our Saviours making such haste to him, they conceived that he was not Dead, but onely in an ordinary sleep, upon the abatement of his disease.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 Then said Jesus unto them plainly, Laza<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rus is dead <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">You will mistake me, my meaning was, not that <ns0:hi>La<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />zarus</ns0:hi> was fallen to rest, upon the abatement of his Distem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />per; but his Soul is parted from his Body.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 And I am glad for your sakes that I was not there <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Had I been upon the place, my kindness to his Sisters, and pity, would have prevailed far with me, to have pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vented his Death; but it is better (for your sake at least) and I am glad I was not there.</ns0:note> (to the intent ye may believe <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">For by this means I shall have an advantage, by putting forth my Divine Power in raising him from the Dead, to confirm your Faith in me as the Son of God, and the true <ns0:hi>Messias</ns0:hi>: therefore, tho he be Dead, let us go unto him.</ns0:note>) never<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />theless, let us go unto him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 Then saith Thomas, which is called Didy<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mus, unto his fellow disciples, Let us also go, that we may die with him <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Thomas</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Didymus</ns0:hi> were names of the same significa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, onely <ns0:hi>Thomas</ns0:hi> was the <ns0:hi>Hebrew,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Didymus</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> name. This is that <ns0:hi>Thomas,</ns0:hi> who to the last, shewed a greater difficulty in believing, than many others of the Dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ciples did, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 20.25. His words here signified great ra<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>hness and unbelief: Let us go and die with him, with Christ (say some). Seeing that our Lord will not be perswad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed from going into <ns0:hi>Iudea,</ns0:hi> where his Life will be in appa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rent danger, for they will put him to death; let us also go and die with him. But it is more probable, that <ns0:hi>Thomas</ns0:hi> meant with <ns0:hi>Lazarus,</ns0:hi> who as our Saviour told them but now was dead; and in that sense, it was not onely an ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pression of <ns0:hi>great passion,</ns0:hi> but great <ns0:hi>unbelief also.</ns0:hi> We ought not to be so affected with the death of our Friends, as to wish, or desire our selves out of the World, where God hath set us in stations, which we ought to keep, until God be pleased to remove us. Besides, <ns0:hi>Thomas</ns0:hi> ought so have believed our Saviour, who had told them, that tho <ns0:hi>Laza<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rus</ns0:hi> slept the sleep of Death, yet he went to <ns0:hi>awake him</ns0:hi>; which could have no other sense, than to raise him out of that sleep of Death, of which he had spoken. Ah! To what Errors do our Passions betray us?</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 Then when Jesus came <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Christ came to <ns0:hi>Bethany</ns0:hi> where <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> died;</ns0:note>, he found that he had lien in the grave four days already <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">He found he had lien in the grave four days, so as pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bably, Christ came not to <ns0:hi>Bethany</ns0:hi> till four days or more after the Death of <ns0:hi>Lazarus,</ns0:hi> or near upon. But possibly, it is better judged by others, that Christ was not yet come into <ns0:hi>Bethany,</ns0:hi> but onely to the place where he met <ns0:hi>Martha</ns0:hi>; because it is said after this, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 30 <ns0:hi>That Iesus</ns0:hi> was not yet come into the Town, but was in that place where <ns0:hi>Martha</ns0:hi> met him; which it is probable, was at <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> his <ns0:hi>Sepul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cher,</ns0:hi> out of the Town, but near it, as all the <ns0:hi>Iewish</ns0:hi> Bu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rying-places were; where he heard from the relation of <ns0:hi>Martha,</ns0:hi> how long <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> had been buried. Our Saviour could have come sooner had he pleased, for tho <ns0:hi>Bethabara</ns0:hi> was on the other side of <ns0:hi>Iordan,</ns0:hi> (so out of the Confines of <ns0:hi>Iudea</ns0:hi>) yet if we may give any credit to those who have laboured in the study of places, it was not above four miles off <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> so as it could not be six miles from <ns0:hi>Bethany,</ns0:hi> which our Saviour could have travelled in a less time than four or five days. Some think <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> dyed the same day news came to Christ of his Sickness; after which we read <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 6. that he stirred not of two days; after which it was <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 7. that he took up thoughts of going into <ns0:hi>Iudea.</ns0:hi> Af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter this, possibly he lingred one or two days, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 14. He tells them <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> was dead. Our Saviour was willing to protract the time, that the Miracle might be more Conspi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cuous and Remarkable.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 (Now Bethany was nigh unto Jerusalem, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">That is a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bout two miles.</ns0:note> a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />about fifteen furlongs off <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">That as we count, wants of two miles half a quar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter.</ns0:note>.)</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 And many of the Jews came to Martha, and Mary, to comfort them concerning their brother <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Not to pray with them for the Soul of their Brother departed. That departed Souls are in a capacity to be ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vantaged by the prayers of their Friends, or any such thing, are corruptions of latter times; but they had a civil usage of mourning for their Friends, the time for which was an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ciently thirty days; they mourned for <ns0:hi>Iacob forty days, Gen.</ns0:hi> 50.3. For <ns0:hi>Aaron thirty days, Numb</ns0:hi> 20.29. So for <ns0:hi>Moses, Deut.</ns0:hi> 34.8. It is probable, the days were fewer for persons of an inferior Quality, but they had some days for all; du<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ring which days, their Neighbours and Friends came to vi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sit them, and relieve them in their sorrow, with such Ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />guments as they had.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 Then Martha, assoon as she heard that Jesus was coming, went and met him <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">It should seem by the story, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 10.41. That <ns0:hi>Martha</ns0:hi> had the care of the House-keeping upon her, <ns0:hi>Mary</ns0:hi> was more Retired; So that the news of Christs coming might come to her first. She in great joy ran out to meet him; how far she went, we are not told; but it appeareth from <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 30. that she went out of the Town.</ns0:note>: but Mary sat <ns0:hi>still</ns0:hi> in the house <ns0:hi>t.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 Then said Martha unto Jesus, Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mary, ver.</ns0:hi> 32. saith the same. They were both in an Error, for <ns0:hi>Lazarus his Death</ns0:hi> was appointed, and determi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned by an Eternal Counsel; and he was both Sick, and died for a wife end, that God might be glorified, and his Son glorified in raising him from the dead; as we were before told <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 4. But it lets us see the vanity of our Natures; who in the loss of our Friends, are ready to think, if such or such means had been used, we had not lost our Friends: never considering our days are appointed, and we cannot pass the number of them. If any rational, probable means for con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tinuing their Lives be omitted, that also is not without the Counsel of God, who having determined the issue, conceal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth diseases, or the true, and proper means for their cure, from <ns0:hi>Physitians,</ns0:hi> or such as are about the Sick persons. Nor did <ns0:hi>Martha</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mary</ns0:hi> fail in this onely, but in that; they made the Lords presence necessary to the preserving of the Life of their Brother; who had he pleased, could (tho absent) have kept him from Death.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 But I know, that even now whatsoever thou wilt ask of God, God will give <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> thee <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">She shewed some unbelief in her former words, but here again the sheweth her Faith, but not without some weakness mixed with her Faith; for by these words she seemeth not to be satisfied, that the fulness of the Godhead dwelt in Christ, and that he was equal with the Father, and able by his own Power to raise the dead; Her Faith extend<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth no farther than a belief, that he was in so much favour with God, that if he would please to Intercede with God, he would restore her Brother to Life; this she meaneth; tho the raising of persons from the dead, was a thing so rare, and unusual, that she dareth not to mention that par<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ticular thing, tho uppermost in her thoughts.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 Jesus saith unto her, Thy brother shall rise again <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Christ takes no notice of <ns0:hi>Martha's</ns0:hi> failings before men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tioned, (He can have compassion upon his peoples Infirmi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ties) but applieth himself to the relief of her under her af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fliction. He doth not tell her, that her Brother should be raised to Life presently, nor that he would do it; but onely saith, <ns0:hi>He shall rise again</ns0:hi>: To let us know, that a belief of the general Resurrection is enough, and ought to be im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />proved by us, to curb our immoderate mourning and Passions for those of our Friends who are dead in the Lord.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 Martha said unto him <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 14.14. Chap. 5.25.</ns0:note>, I know that he shall rise again in the Resurrection at the last day <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">From hence we learn, that the general <ns0:hi>Resurrection of the Dead,</ns0:hi> is no novel Doctrine; <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> believed it, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 19.26, 27. <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> published it, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 12.1. The <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> owned it, tho the <ns0:hi>Sadduces</ns0:hi> denied it; and possibly the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> had but a confused Notion of it. <ns0:hi>Martha</ns0:hi> here makes it an Article of her Faith.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 6.3<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> life <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Martha</ns0:hi> by her speech seemed not to have a true Notion of Christ; She believed that there should be a general Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />surrection from the dead in the last day, by the mighty Power of God, but she did not truly understand, what in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fluence Christ had <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> this Resurrection, that the raising of the Dead, should be the peculiar Work of Christ, not without the Father, but as he was Ordained by the Father, to be the Judge of the Q<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ick and of the Dead. Christ doth therefore here further instruct her, and tell her, He was the <ns0:hi>Resurrection</ns0:hi>; where (as is usual in Scripture) the <ns0:hi>Effect</ns0:hi> is put for the <ns0:hi>Cause: I am the Resurrection,</ns0:hi> is no more, than I am, and shall be, the <ns0:hi>Principal Cause</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Resurrection</ns0:hi>: The Dead shall hear the Voice of the Son of God, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 5.28. He also adds, <ns0:hi>and the Life</ns0:hi>; That is, the cause of Life: both that Life which the Dead shall in the Resurrection re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cover, and also that <ns0:hi>Eternal Life</ns0:hi> which shall follow.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 3.36. 1 John 5.10.</ns0:note> he that beleiveth in me, tho he were dead, yet shall he live <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">And whosoever looketh upon me in that Notion, and committeth himself unto me, tho he doth dye, yet he shall Rise again, and <ns0:hi>Live Eternally</ns0:hi>; and this Power being in me, I am not tyed to the last day, but have a Power when I please to Raise the Dead. Our Saviour indeed hath more in his Answer than respected the present case, but there was nothing more usual with him, than in his discourses to raise up the hearts of his People to higher things, as he doth in this place raise <ns0:hi>Martha</ns0:hi> beyond the thoughts of a Resurrection of her Bro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers Body to a Natural Life, to the thoughts of a Spiritual and Eternal Life.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:353" />26 And whosoever liveth <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">He had before proved himself to be the <ns0:hi>Resurrection,</ns0:hi> now he proveth himself to be <ns0:hi>the Life.</ns0:hi> He saith, he that Liveth, that Liveth a Natural Life, if he be one who receiv<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth and imbraceth me as the true <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> and Saviour of the World, and committeth himself, and all the concerns of his Soul to me, shall never die, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.11. Tho his body shall die because of Sin, yet his Spirit shall live because of Righteousness; and God shall in the great Day quicken a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />again his mortal Body, through the holy Spirit which dwell<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth in him, and is united to him.</ns0:note>, and believeth in me, shall never die <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">He asketh <ns0:hi>Martha</ns0:hi> if she believed this. We shall observe, that our Saviour, not here onely, but <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 9.22.28. before he wrought his Mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />raculous Operations, required Peoples <ns0:hi>Faith</ns0:hi> as a prerequi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />site. And <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 13.58. He could not do many mighty Works in his own Country, because of their unbelief. And <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 17.20. He tells his Disciples, that the reason why they could not cure the man Possessed with the Devil, was, because of their unbelief: So great an honour hath God given to the exercise of Faith.</ns0:note>. Believest thou this <ns0:hi>d</ns0:hi>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 She saith unto him, Yea Lord <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 4.4<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. and 6 69.</ns0:note>: I believe that thou art the Christ the Son of God which should come into the world <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">This is the nearest to the Confession of <ns0:hi>Peter, Matth.</ns0:hi> 16.16. Which our Saviour calleth, <ns0:hi>The Rock upon which he would build his Church,</ns0:hi> of any that we have in Scripture; yea, and more full than that; for those words, <ns0:hi>which should come into the World,</ns0:hi> are not in <ns0:hi>Peters</ns0:hi> Confession. The sum of this is, <ns0:hi>Martha</ns0:hi> doth here profess a full assent to our Saviour as the <ns0:hi>Messias,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Son of God</ns0:hi>; he who was Prefigured, Prophesied of, Promised, as he who should come into the World.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 And when she had so said, she went her way, and called Mary her sister secretly, saying, The Master is come and calleth for thee <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mary</ns0:hi> was left at home, while <ns0:hi>Martha</ns0:hi> went out of the Town to meet Christ: It seemeth by this verse, Christ had asked for her, (tho that be not mentioned before) <ns0:hi>Martha</ns0:hi> goeth secretly to her, and tells her, that the <ns0:hi>Master</ns0:hi> was come: (It was a Name they usually called their most Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mous Teachers by.)</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 Assoon as she <ns0:hi>heard that, she arose</ns0:hi> quickly, and came unto him <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Maries</ns0:hi> love and readiness to attend upon Christ, ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />peareth by a former story concerning her and her Sister <ns0:hi>Martha,</ns0:hi> Recorded <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 10.38, 39, 40. But the present sorrow she was in for her dead <ns0:hi>Brother,</ns0:hi> together with the hopes she conceived of having him restored to Life by Christs coming, added wings to her motion; therefore the Evan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gelist saith, she arose quickly, and came to him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 Now Jesus was not yet come into the town, but was in that place where Martha met him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 The Jews then which were with her in the house, and comforted her, when they saw Ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry that she rose up hastily and went forth, fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lowed her, saying, She goeth unto the grave, to weep there.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 Then when Mary was come where Jesus was, and saw him, she fell down at his feet <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">she <ns0:hi>falls down at his feet,</ns0:hi> which was a po<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sture; (as we have heard before) very usual in those Coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tries, by which they testified, both their civil Respects to Princes, and Great Persons, and also which they used in the Worship of God, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 2.11. Whether <ns0:hi>Mary</ns0:hi> did it upon the one account or the othe<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, dependeth upon what we cannot know; <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> Whether she at this time was f<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>lly per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />swaded of his Divine Nature; of which the best of the Dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ciples till Christs Resurrection, had but <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> faint and uncer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain perswasion.</ns0:note>, say<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing unto him, Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The words which she useth to him, are the same, which <ns0:hi>Martha</ns0:hi> used, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 21. (See the Notes there).</ns0:note>.<ns0:note place="bottom">Coming,</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 When Jesus therefore saw her weep<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>ng, and the Jews also weeping which came with her, he groaned in the spirit, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. He trou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bled himself.</ns0:note> was troubled <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The Apostle speaks of Christ, Heb. 4.15. <ns0:hi>as an High Pri<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>st, that can be touched with the feeling of our Infirmi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ties,</ns0:hi> and one <ns0:hi>that can have compassion, Heb.</ns0:hi> 5.2. <ns0:hi>Martha's</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>M<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ry's</ns0:hi> Passion for their dead <ns0:hi>Brother</ns0:hi> was their Infir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mity; Christ is touched with the feeling of it. He to shew himself truly man, <ns0:hi>groaned in himself</ns0:hi>; it being natural to us, to be affected with the afflictions of others, and to weep with those who weep. But here ariseth a question, <ns0:hi>Whether Christ was troubled from a Natural necessity, as we some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times cannot forbear weeping, to see others weep bitterly; or out of choice?</ns0:hi> Some of the Ancients think it was out of choice. Mr. <ns0:hi>Calvin</ns0:hi> and others think, that it was out of a Natural necessity; not that he could not govern his Passions (as we sometimes cannot) by reason; but that he could not as man forbear his Passion. I shall Translate what Mr. <ns0:hi>Calvin</ns0:hi> speaks most judiciously in the case, determining nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther way, but leaving it to the Readers judgment. <ns0:hi>But how (saith he) do gnawing, and trouble of Spirit, agree to that Person who was the Son of God? Because, to some it looketh very absurd to say, that Christ as one of us, is subject to human Passions; they think Christ no otherwise at any time, either grieved or rejoiced, than as he, so often as he thought fit, voluntarily assumed to himself those Passions by a secret dispensation.</ns0:hi> Augustine <ns0:hi>thought that Christ in this sense is said to have groaned, and to have been troubled; whereas, other mens Passions Transport them, and exercise a Tyranny over them, to the disturbance of their minds: he therefore thinks the meaning is, That Christ being otherwise sedate, and free from Passions, sometimes voluntarily took these Passions. But (saith he) in my judgment, it is a much plainer and simpler sense of this Scripture, if <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e say, That the Son of God, taking upon him our Nature, did also freely with it, put on our Affections</ns0:hi>; (which are our Natu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tural Infirmities) <ns0:hi>so as he in nothing differed from us, but in this, that he had no Sin. Nothing by this is derogated from the Glory of Christ; for he voluntarily submitted to take our Nature upon him: by which he became like to us in our Hu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mane Affections. And we must not think, that after he had voluntarily submitted to take our perfect Nature upon him, that he was free from the Passions and Affections of it: in this he proved himself to be our Brother, that we might know that he is a Mediator for us, who can easily pardon our Infirmities, and is ready to help us, as to those Infirmities which he hath experienced in his own Person. If any one object, That seeing our Passions are Sinful, it doth not agree to the Nature of him who was the Son of God, to share with us in them. I Answer, saith he, There is a great deal of dif<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ference</ns0:hi> (as to these Passions) <ns0:hi>betwixt us, and Christ; for our Affections are therefore faulty, because they are intem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />perate, and inordinate, and keep no bounds; but in Christ, tho they be, yet they are Composed, and moderate, and in O<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bedience to God. The Passions of men are faulty upon two accounts,</ns0:hi> 1 As they are Turbulent, <ns0:hi>and not Governed by the Rule of moderation.</ns0:hi> 2 As they often rise without any due ground or foundation, <ns0:hi>or are not</ns0:hi> directed to a right end. <ns0:hi>They are in us a disease, because we neither grieve, nor re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />joice in measure: and to that degree alone, which God per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mits and allows, many rather give the reins to their Passi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons. And such is the Vanity of our minds, that we are grie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved and troubled for little or no causes, being too much ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dicted, and cleaving to the World. There was no such thing in Christ, no Passion in him ever exceeded its just bounds, or was exercised, but upon a just and reasonable cause. To make this yet cle<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>rer, we must distinguish betwixt man in his Creation, and the Degenerate Nature of man, as it is corrupted through Sin: When God at first Created man, he Created him with Natural Affection<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                        <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> but such as were un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der the command of Reason: That our Pa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>sions are now in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ordinate, and rebellious, is accidental to our Natu<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e. Christ indeed took our Affections upon him, but without that disor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der which fell into them by the Fall, which causeth us that we cannot obey them and God. He was greatly troubled, but not so as by his trouble to become disobedient to his Father. In short, if we compare our Affections with his, there will ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pear as great a difference, as betwixt pure water, and that which is dirty and filthy. And the single example of Christ, is enough to make us reject the Stoi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="3 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> [<ns0:hi>or</ns0:hi> want of Passion] <ns0:hi>for from whom, if not from him, should we fetch the highest Rule of Perfection? Let us therefore rather study to Correct, and Tame that disorder, in which our Passions are intangled, and follow Christ as our guide, that we may bring them into order: Thus</ns0:hi> Paul, 1 Thes. 4.13. <ns0:hi>doth not require of us a stony stupidity, but commands us to Govern our grief, that we may not mourn as men without hope. For Christ therefore took our Affections upon him, that we by his Grace may be inabled to subdue whatsoever is vitious in them.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:354" />34 And said, Where have ye laid him? They say unto him, Lord, come and see.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="35">35 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luk. 19.41.</ns0:note> Jesus <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>ept <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Weeping is not of it self a Sinful, but Natural Passion, which (as was said before) doth very well agree with Christ, having voluntarily taken upon him our Nature, and Natu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ral Infirmities.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="36">36 Then said the Jews, Behold how he loved him <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Love sheweth it self as in a complacence in the object beloved, while we injoy it; so in a grief for it when we are deprived of it: The <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> therefore rightly concluded Christs kindness to <ns0:hi>Lazarus,</ns0:hi> from his human Affection expressed at his Death</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="37">37 And some of them said <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Some onely concluded Christs love to the deceased, from his Affection shewed at his grave; but others make a worse conclusion</ns0:note>, Could not this man <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 9.6.</ns0:note>, which opened the eyes of the blind, have caused that even this man should not have died <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">in derogation to Christs Reputation, from the miracle he had wrought, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 9. in restoring him that was born Blind; for their speech soundeth in this sense; if he had indeed cured one that was born Blind, cer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tainly, he could as well have kept this man, to whom (dead) he expresseth so great Affection, clear from Death. A Learn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed Interpreter therefore calleth this, a <ns0:hi>Devilish Sarcasm</ns0:hi>; they go about to weaken the Reputation of our Saviour, from the miracle which he had wrought, apparently shew<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing his Divine Power, because he did not keep his Friend from dying. It is much like the scoff with which they after<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward scoffed him, while he hung upon the Cross <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 27.42. <ns0:hi>He saved others, himself he could not save</ns0:hi>: Or the words may have been spoke, if not with an Irony, yet with Admi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ration; that having cured the Blind man, a Stranger to him, he did not heal his Sick Friend: or as if they were uncer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain whether his Power of Working miracles, were not limited to some times, that he could not perform all things when he pleased. But how weak must this their Argumen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tation be, which could stand upon no other foundation than this: <ns0:hi>That if Christ were the Son of God, he would at all times, and in all cases, have put forth his Divine Power</ns0:hi>? As if God acted necessarily, not freely, Governing his Actions by his own Wisdom, as he saw most conducing to the wise ends of his own glory.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="38">38 Jesus therefore again groaning in himself <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">As before, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 33. So shewing himself yet further to be truly man, and not without human Affections; he cometh to the place where <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> his Dead Body was laid, which the Evangelist telleth us was a <ns0:hi>Cave,</ns0:hi> or a hollow place in the Earth, or some Rock.</ns0:note>, cometh to the grave. It was a cave, and a stone lay upon it <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">And they were wont to roll some great Stones to the mouth of those graves, (as we see in the burial of our Saviour, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 27.66.)</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="39">39 Jesus said, Take ye away the stone <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Our Lord commandeth the removal of the Stone, which was at the mouth of the Sepulcher, that the miracle might be evident, for <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> to have come forth; the door of the Cave being shut, and a great Stone making it fast, would have looked more like an Apparition, than a Resur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rection.</ns0:note> Martha, the sister of him that was dead, saith unto him, Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been <ns0:hi>dead</ns0:hi> four days <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">It is very probable, that <ns0:hi>Martha</ns0:hi> thought that our Saviour commanded the removal of the Stone, not in order to a commanding him to Life again, but out of a cu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />riosity to view his Dead Body: and therefore she objecteth the Pu<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>refaction of his Body, from which the Soul was now departed four days; as that which our Saviour would not be able to indure the savour of.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="40">40 Jesus saith unto her, Said I not unto thee, That, if thou wouldest believe, thou shouldest see the glory of God <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Christ now beginneth to open to <ns0:hi>Martha</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mary,</ns0:hi> and the rest, his resolution to raise <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> from the Dead by and by. Christ saith that to us in his word, which he saith by a just consequence, tho he doth not speak it in so many words: we do not read in this History, that Christ had spo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ken this in so many words and syllables, but he had spoken it in effect; he had told her, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 25. that <ns0:hi>He was the Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />surrection and the Life,</ns0:hi> that he had Power to raise Dead Bodies from a Natural Death to Life; and that for those <ns0:hi>who believed in him, tho they were dead, they should live.</ns0:hi> This could not be without a great manifestation of the glory of God: the Power of God is his glory. <ns0:hi>Once have I spo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ken</ns0:hi> (saith the <ns0:hi>Psalmist) yea, twice have I heard it, that</ns0:hi> Power <ns0:hi>belongs to God.</ns0:hi> Thou shouldest see God by me manifesting the glory of his Almighty Power; God glori<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fying himself, and glorifying his Son. Believing brings us in experiences of God; whereas unbelief, as it were, limiteth God, and tieth up his hands.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="41">41 Then they took away the stone <ns0:hi>from the place,</ns0:hi> where the dead was laid <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">The Servants, or Friends about the grave, removed the Stone from the mouth of the Cave, within which the Dead Corps of <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> lay.</ns0:note>. And Jesus lift up <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> eyes <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">Christ before his Thanksgiving to his Father, is said to have <ns0:hi>lifted up his eyes</ns0:hi>; a posture often used in mens addresses to God, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 121<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>1. and 123.1. as an indication of their belief, that <ns0:hi>Heaven is Gods Throne</ns0:hi>: tho he filleth Heaven and Earth, yet the Heaven is his Court where he most gloriously sheweth himself, the Earth but his footstool.</ns0:note>, and said, Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">We read here of nothing that Christ had said before; yet he giveth Thanks here to his Father, that he had <ns0:hi>heard him.</ns0:hi> The meaning is, Thou hast Willed, or pleased to grant those things which I desired. It is very hard to determine, whether Christ had used some audible words before this, upon this occasion, in Prayer to his Father, which the Evangelist could not, or did not set down: or whether he onely <ns0:hi>groaned in his Spirit,</ns0:hi> (as was said be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore). By those groans (not onely expressing his sorrow for <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> his Death, or rather sympathy with the Affli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctions of <ns0:hi>Mary</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Martha</ns0:hi>) but also his desires to his Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, that he might be again restored to Life; and his se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cond <ns0:hi>groaning, ver.</ns0:hi> 38. was of that Nature, which groanings in the Saints, God understandeth, <ns0:hi>knowing the mind of the Spirit,</ns0:hi> making Intercession for <ns0:hi>the Saints, according to the Will of God.</ns0:hi> (As the Apostle teacheth us, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.27.) much more did the Father, (who was one in <ns0:hi>Nature, Essence,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Will</ns0:hi> with the <ns0:hi>Son</ns0:hi>) understand them in him. Nothing in these cases can be determined, much less can any conclude from hence, that there is no need of our using any words in our Prayers; for, altho there be no simple absolute necessi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty, that we should use them in order to Gods Knowledge of what we need, and would have; for he that searcheth the Heart, knows what we need, and what we desire, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 6.8. yet there is a necessity for our words, in order to ou<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> obey<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing Gods command, <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 14.2. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 11.2. There is a great deal of difference betwixt Gods hearing of Christ, and hearing us: Christ and his Father have one Essence, one Nature, and Will.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="42">42 And I knew that thou hearest me al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ways <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">I know that thou always Willest those things which I Will, and I Will nothing but what thou Willest, and hast sent me to do in the World; so as in these things it is im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />possible, but that thou shouldest always be ready to grant what I ask of thee; nay, there is no need of my asking.</ns0:note>: but <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap 12 <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> because of the people which stand by, I said it, that they may believe that thou hast sent me <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">I onely give thee thanks for the Peoples sake, who here stand by, who believe thee to be the true God, and to have an Almighty Power; but will not as yet believe that I am thy Son, by thee sent into the World; and that I do the works which I do in thee, and from thee. We read of many mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />racles wrought by Christ, without any Prayer first put up to his Father, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 8.2. and 9.6. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 5.41. and 9.25. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 7.14. using onely an Authorative word; nor need he have used any here, but onely for the further con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viction of the People, that he was sent of God, that God whom they owned as their God: he Prayeth and giveth Thanks to God before them all.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="43">43 And when he had thus spoken <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">When he had groaned in his Spirit, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> audibly given Thanks to his Father for hearing of him, and testified, that he did this, not because he ever had any <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> of his Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers Willing what he Will'd, but that the People might take notice of his Favour, and Power with God, and sent of him.</ns0:note>, he cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                     <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap> 
                  <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">He <ns0:hi>cried</ns0:hi> with a <ns0:hi>loud Voice,</ns0:hi> not whispering, nor like <ns0:hi>Wizzards peeping</ns0:hi> and muttering, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 8.19. but speaking aloud, so as all might hear, and understand, that what was done, was done by his Powerful Word: he calls him by his Name, he bids him come forth; they were not the words that raised <ns0:hi>Lazarus,</ns0:hi> but the mighty quickning Power of Christ, which attended these words.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="44">44 And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with grave-clothes: and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>is face was bound about with a napkin <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The fashion of their dressing up the Dead differeth, ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cording to the fashion of several Countries; among the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> we understand by this text<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> they tied a <ns0:hi>napkin</ns0:hi> about their <ns0:hi>head,</ns0:hi> and some <ns0:hi>clothes</ns0:hi> about their <ns0:hi>hands</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>feet.</ns0:hi> They wound the whole <ns0:hi>Body with linnen clothes, Chap.</ns0:hi> 19.40. with Spices; this was, (as is there said) their manner to bury. So <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 5.6. The young men are said to have <ns0:hi>wound Ananias,</ns0:hi> and carried him out, and buried him; and this is that which certainly is meant here by these words, <ns0:hi>bound hand and foot</ns0:hi>: and here is a second miracle, that one so wrapped, and bound up, should be able to move and come forth.</ns0:note>. Jesus saith unto them<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Loose him, and let him go <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Christ bids <ns0:hi>loose him,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>let him go,</ns0:hi> to evidence him truly recovered to Life again, and that the miracle was perfectly wrought. About this miracle there are two cur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ious questions started, 1. <ns0:hi>Whether the raising of Lazarus to Life, was done by the meer Divine Power of Christ, or by the Person of Christ; so as the human Nature, being Personally Vnited to the Divine Nature, had also a share in it: the Di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vine Nature communicating its property of quickning the Dead, to the human Nature</ns0:hi>? That it was the Person of Christ that raised <ns0:hi>Lazarus,</ns0:hi> and he who did it, was truly man, and <ns0:hi>truly God,</ns0:hi> is out of doubt. But that there was any such Communication of the properties of the Divine Nature to the Human Nature, that it also had a share in this effect, is just<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly denied, and doubted by many great Divines: but it is a question tending to no great profit for us to know. A se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cond is, <ns0:hi>Where Lazarus his Soul was, these four days wherein it was separated from the Body?</ns0:hi> The Scripture hath not told us this, and it speaks too great curiosity to inquire too strictly. Tho we are taught from the Parable of <ns0:hi>Dives</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Lazarus,</ns0:hi> that the Souls of departed Saints<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> do ordina<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rily and immediately pass into Heaven, or <ns0:hi>Abrahams</ns0:hi> bo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />some; yet what should hinder, but that in these cases, where it appears to have been the Divine Will, that the Souls of persons departed should again be returned into their bodies in a short time; they might by a Divine Power be kept un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der the custody of Angels, until the time of such Restaurati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on of them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="45">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:354" />45 Then many of the Jews which came to Ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry, and had seen the things which Jesus did <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">That is, which came to visit <ns0:hi>Martha</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mary</ns0:hi> in their mourning; and coming to <ns0:hi>Mary,</ns0:hi> did go along with her to the Sepulcher to meet Christ, and there meeting him, saw all the passages relating to this miracle</ns0:note>, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieved on him <ns0:note n="f," place="bottom">truly believed on him as the true <ns0:hi>Messiah, Chap.</ns0:hi> 12.11, 18. Or it may be, it is to be understood more largely of such a <ns0:hi>Faith</ns0:hi> as is but a preparatory to true and saving Faith; for there was a double use of miracles, 1. To prepare men for Faith, dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />posing them to give an ear to him, to whom God had given so great a Power: so as after the sight of them, they were more fitted to hear, and inclinable to believe. 2. To <ns0:hi>con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />f<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>rm Faith</ns0:hi> in those that believed, so as they believed the more firmly, seeing the Doctrine they heard, confirmed by such miraculous Operations.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="46">46 But some of them went their ways to the Pharisees, and told them what things Jesus had done <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">These <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> had the same means for believing, the others had; they had heard the same words from Christ, they had seen the same miracle wrought by Christ. Whence is it that any of the other <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> believed? these, instead of believing, run to the Pharisees to accuse him. Can any account be gi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven of this, unless from the freedom of Divine Grace, shew<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing mercy where God will shew mercy? Tho possibly the former wickedness of these <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> was the cause of Gods not giving that Grace to them, which he gave to others.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="47">47 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 2.2. Matth. 26.3. Mar. 14.1.</ns0:note> Then gathered the chief priests and the Pharisees a council, and said, What <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 12.19. Acts 4.16.</ns0:note> do we? for this man doth many miracles <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>chief Priests</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> were a great part of that great Council amongst the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> which went under the name of the <ns0:hi>Sanhedrim</ns0:hi>; and this (probably) was the <ns0:hi>Council</ns0:hi> they gathered; for <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 49. we read, that <ns0:hi>Caiphas</ns0:hi> the High Priest, the standing President of that Court, was a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mongst them. The miracles wrought by Christ, were the things that disturbed them, and they reflect upon themselves for conniving so long at him; what they should have im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />proved, (<ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> the miracles which he wrought) to have be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />got or increased Faith in them; they mention, and mi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />prove to their destruction.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="48">48 If we let him thus alone, all men will believe on him <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">They are afraid, that if they should any longer suffer Christ to go on working miracles, he would have a great many followers, who upon the credit of his miracles, would own him as the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> and the effect and consequence of this would be, they should by the <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi> (to whom they were already in subjection) be utterly deprived of that little liberty they indulged them.</ns0:note>, and the Romans shall come and take a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />way both our place and nation <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">They say, the <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi> would come, (that is with an Army) and destroy their <ns0:hi>Temple,</ns0:hi> which they call <ns0:hi>their Place,</ns0:hi> their most famous Place, where they met to worship God, and in which as a token of Gods presence amongst them, they so much glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ried; yea, and their Nation; that is, miserably destroy their Na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, and bring it to utter Ruine, whether they really thought so or no, or onely spake this as an Argument to hasten the Death of Christ, is not much material for us to know. There was this colour for it, The <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> were a People very prone upon all occasions to <ns0:hi>Rebel,</ns0:hi> and Rise up in the defence of their liberties, when ever they could get any Head, to give them any countenance and Conduct. They also lived in a general expectation of the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> when the Scepter should be departed from <ns0:hi>Iuda,</ns0:hi> (as it now was) and when <ns0:hi>Daniels seventy Weeks</ns0:hi> mentioned, <ns0:hi>Chap</ns0:hi> 9.24. should be determined, which were now fulfilled; so as there was about this time, a general expectation of the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> of whom also it is ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />parent they had a false Notion, and generally expected un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der the Notion of the <ns0:hi>Messiah</ns0:hi>; not the Son of God taking Human Nature, and to die for their Redemption, and then rise again from the Dead, and Ascend into Heaven; but a <ns0:hi>Tem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />poral Prince,</ns0:hi> who Conquering all their Enemies, should deliver them from all Captivities and Servitudes, and restore them to their ancient liberties. This their expectation was known well enough to the <ns0:hi>Roman</ns0:hi> Governors, (as appeareth by <ns0:hi>Herods</ns0:hi> question to the Wise men in <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 2.4.) and they were very jealous of the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> on this account, which caused <ns0:hi>Herods</ns0:hi> Bloody Act in killing the Children in and about <ns0:hi>Bethlehem:</ns0:hi> So as the Rulers of the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> (according to the Notion they had of the <ns0:hi>Messiah</ns0:hi>) might reasonably think, that if Christ were taken to be, and he went on confirming the opinion of himself by these miracles, so as People gene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rally ran after him: the <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi> would reasonably suppose they had a design to <ns0:hi>Rebel,</ns0:hi> and therefore would come upon them, destroy their Temple, and utterly Ruine their Nation. But how will they avoid this? That which they agreed up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on we shall meet with <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 53<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>They took Counsel to put him to death.</ns0:hi> How they were led on to that fatal Counsel, we shall hear.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="49">49 And one of them <ns0:hi>named</ns0:hi> Caiphas, being the high priest that same year <ns0:hi>l,</ns0:hi> said unto them, Ye know nothing at all <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">The High Priest by the Divine Law was to be but one, and he the Eldest Son of <ns0:hi>Aarons</ns0:hi> House; nor was he to be for a year, but for his Life, as appeareth by a multitude of Texts in the Books of <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi>; but all things were now out of order in the <ns0:hi>Iewish</ns0:hi> Church; they were under the Power of the <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi>; all places, especially that of the High Priest<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> were bought and sold amongst them: some say, they had two High Priests, others say but one, onely he had an assi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stant, called by that name, that had a Partnership in the Honour. After <ns0:hi>Herods</ns0:hi> time there was no regard to the Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mily of <ns0:hi>Aaron,</ns0:hi> or the <ns0:hi>Asmoneans,</ns0:hi> but the <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi> made what High Priest they pleased; so as <ns0:hi>Iosephus</ns0:hi> tells us, that the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> who had but thirteen High Priests from <ns0:hi>Aarons</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Solomons</ns0:hi> time, which was six hundred and twelve years; nor more than eighteen in four hundred and sixty years after, to the Captivity of <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi>; nor more than fifteen from thence, to the time of <ns0:hi>Antiochus,</ns0:hi> which was four hundred and four<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teen years; had twenty eight betwixt the time that <ns0:hi>Herod</ns0:hi> began to Reign, and <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> was destroyed, of which this <ns0:hi>Caiphas</ns0:hi> was one, and certainly the chief, (if there were two at this time) and consequently the President of their great Court, whom all attended to, and his words went a great way with the rest<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">He chargeth the rest of the Council with folly, as not considering what was fit to be done.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="50">50 Nor consider that it is expedient for us <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap 18.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note>, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Never was any thing spoken more Diabolically; He re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gards not what was their duty, nor what was lawful for them to do; whether they might upon any pretence shed Innocent blood, much more the blood of one whose Life was spent in nothing but a going up and down in doing good: Onely<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>like a wretched Polititian, who was concerned for nothing but the peoples Safety; he saith not <ns0:hi>it is lawful,</ns0:hi> but it is expedient for us that one man, be he never so good, never so Innocent and Just, should die for the people, that is, to save the whole Nation from destruction.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="51">51 And this spake he not of himself <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">So far as this was a Prophecy, he spake not of himself; take the words of <ns0:hi>Caiphas</ns0:hi> in the sense that he spake them, they were such as might well enough come out of such a wretched mouth, speaking out of the abundance of a vile and wretched heart, <ns0:hi>Melius pereat unus q<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>m unitas.</ns0:hi> That it was better that one man should die, let him be never so Good, Just and Innocent, than that for his sake mischief should come upon a Nation. This was now sutable enough to the Religion of such an <ns0:hi>High Priest</ns0:hi>: But that in this (the words being capable of a double sense) <ns0:hi>Caiphas</ns0:hi> should deliver a great truth; That this year <ns0:hi>One should die for the people</ns0:hi>; that is, <ns0:hi>The Messiah should be cut off, but not for himself,</ns0:hi> as we read <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 9.26. This was no more from himself, than the words which <ns0:hi>Balaams</ns0:hi> Ass spake were from its self. The <ns0:hi>Spirit of Prophecy</ns0:hi> sometimes fell upon wicked men; God revealed to <ns0:hi>Pharaoh</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Nebuchadnezzar,</ns0:hi> (both which were <ns0:hi>Pagans</ns0:hi>) the things which he intended to do<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> There was a time also when <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> (tho a man rejected of God) did also Prophecy; and the worst of the Princes of <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> had an use of the <ns0:hi>Vrim</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Thummim.</ns0:hi> So also here <ns0:hi>Ca<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>phas,</ns0:hi> tho a vile and wicked man, was here influenced by God to Prophecy, and speak an <ns0:hi>Oracle:</ns0:hi> nor are those wo<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>s [<ns0:hi>being High Priest that year</ns0:hi>] superfluously put in, for it being consi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>tent with the Holiness of God, sometimes <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>o make use of the Tongues of the worst of men to declare his Will, it seems agreeable to the Wisdom of God in doing it, to make use of principal men, they being Persons whose words are most likely to be regarded, and so make impression upon people. The <ns0:hi>Papists</ns0:hi> would from hence infer the i<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>fa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ibility of the <ns0:hi>Pope,</ns0:hi> because he is the <ns0:hi>High Priest</ns0:hi>: but they ought to prove, 1. <ns0:hi>That the Office of the Pope,</ns0:hi> hath any foundation in the word of God. 2. <ns0:hi>That this was a gift given to particular Priests,</ns0:hi> and at particular times; for the <ns0:hi>Iewish</ns0:hi> High Priests were fallible enough or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dinarily, witness <ns0:hi>Aarons</ns0:hi> making the golden Calf, and <ns0:hi>Vri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jah</ns0:hi> the Altar after the pattern of <ns0:hi>Damascus,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 16.10, 11. The words, <ns0:hi>being High Priest,</ns0:hi> are not given as a reason why <ns0:hi>Caiphas</ns0:hi> Prophecied, tho they are a good rea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son why God was pleased to chose his Tongue, and over-rule it beyond his own thoughts and intentions, to serve his design in this Revelation. He did not Prophecy intentionally, as de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />signing such a thing onely <ns0:hi>materially</ns0:hi>; the matter of his words were indeed a <ns0:hi>Divine Revelation,</ns0:hi> tho his intention and scope was fit for none but a base, carnal Politician. God made him a Prophet in what he said, tho he meant not so.</ns0:note>: for being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus should die fot that nation <ns0:hi>p:</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="52">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:355" />52 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 49.6.</ns0:note> not for that nation onely <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Not for the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> onely. The words used in <ns0:hi>Caiphas</ns0:hi> his speech were <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> and <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, words not significant of the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> onely, but of other people also:</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Eph. 2.14, 15<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 16.</ns0:note> but that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">for Christ was to gather into one body all the <ns0:hi>Elect of God,</ns0:hi> (who are here called the children of God, because they were to be so after their being begotten by the Immortal seed of the Word, and born again of Water and the Spirit) those that at present were scattered abroad over the face of the whole Earth: Christ, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.10. was to gather in one all things in Heaven and Earth. The Evangelist extendeth the sense of <ns0:hi>Caiphas</ns0:hi> his Prophecy, to <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> as well as <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> according to the exte<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t of the Death of Christ, declared 1 <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 2.2.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="53">53 Then from that day forth they took coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sel together for to put him to death <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">They had taken such Counsels before; but now they were more intent than before, having found a juster pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tence, <ns0:hi>viz</ns0:hi> to prevent a Sedition and Rebellion; and learn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed of their <ns0:hi>High Priest,</ns0:hi> that it was more convenient that one should die, than that a whole Nation should be destroy<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed. The High Priest had satisfied their Consciences: now they make all the hast they can to put their malicious de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />signs in execution.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="54">54 Jesus therefore <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 4.1, 3. and 7.1.</ns0:note> walked no more openly amongst the Jews <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">For he being the true Paschal Lamb, was to be slain at that Feast, and put an end to that Type, and would there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore reserve h<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>mse<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>f for that time, which was now at hand.</ns0:note>: but went thence unto a countrey near to the wilderness, into a city call<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed Ephraim <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">What this <ns0:hi>Ephren</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Ephraim</ns0:hi> was, Interpreters vainly bu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sie themselves in inquiring; it was some obscure City, and near the Wilderness; some think it was in the Lot of <ns0:hi>Ben<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jamin,</ns0:hi> others think it was within the Lot of <ns0:hi>Ephraim,</ns0:hi> and obtained its name from the Tribe within whose Lot it was. The Scripture no where mentioneth it: and it cannot be ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pected, but that in so many changes of Government as had befallen the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> the names of places should be so altered, that we should be at loss for many of them:</ns0:note>, and there continued with his dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ciples <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">where ever it was, it is said that Christ and his Disciples continued there in some privacy.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="55">55 And the Jews passover was nigh at hand <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Christs last Passover, which was the fourth after he had entred upon his publick Ministry, this was nigh:</ns0:note>, and many went out of the countrey up to Je<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rusalem before the passover to purifie them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">He doth not say all, but <ns0:hi>many</ns0:hi> went up to purifie themselves. There was no general legal purification required before men did eat the Passover: but there were several legal uncleannesses, and purifications necessary to cleanse men from them; now those who had any special <ns0:hi>Purification</ns0:hi> to pass, went before others, that they might have time to do what the Law re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quired of them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="56">56 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 7.11.</ns0:note> Then sought they for Jesus, and spake among themselves, as they stood in the temple, VVhat think ye? that he will not come to the feast <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">I find good Interpreters expounding <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 6. of the friends of Christ, who having used to meet Christ at these Feasts, and see some Miracles wrought by him, did out of a good design seek for him, and inquire of each other, whe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther they knew, whether he intended to be at the Feast; yet it may also be understood of his Enemies, tho it seemeth some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing too early, being six or seven days before.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="57">57 Now both the chief priests and the Pharisees had given a commandment, that if any man knew where he were, he should shew <ns0:hi>it,</ns0:hi> that they might take him <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">For their great Court had issued out orders for the dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />covery and apprehending of our Saviour, if they cou<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>d any way learn where he was. This was in pursuance of that wicked Counsel of which we read before, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 33. there they decreed: now they cannot rest until they bring their bloody devices to pass, for which we shall soon find God giving them an opportunity.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
